dx: Downward lens dislocation in classic homocystinuria
case: A 12-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of blurred distance vision that has worsened over the past year. She has mild intellectual disability and had a deep venous thrombosis of the left leg at age 10 years. She is at the 97th percentile for height and has long, thin limbs. Her joints are not hypermobile. Slit-lamp examination shows both lenses displaced inferiorly. Plasma total homocysteine is 180 µmol/L (normal 5 to 15), and plasma methionine is increased. Serum vitamin B12 and folate concentrations are within the reference ranges. Genetic testing confirms cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency. She is diagnosed with classic homocystinuria with bilateral downward lens dislocation.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the displacement of this patient's lenses?
options: Raised intraocular pressure pushing the lens forward
Weakened zonular fibers containing abnormal fibrillin
Contraction of the ciliary muscle pulling the lens down
Swelling of the lens from sorbitol accumulation
approach: The lens hangs from the ciliary body by zonular fibers (the suspensory ligament). A lens can only shift position if those fibers stretch or break.
Zonular fibers are built mostly from fibrillin-1, a protein held together by many disulfide bonds between cysteine residues.
Very high homocysteine reacts with those cysteine residues and disrupts fibrillin, so the zonules weaken and the lens drops.
questions.why: In homocystinuria, excess homocysteine damages the cysteine-rich fibrillin in the zonular fibers. The weakened zonules let go, and the lens usually slips downward (inferiorly or inferonasally). Marfan syndrome also weakens zonules through a fibrillin-1 gene defect, but there the lens usually moves upward. The direction of dislocation and the clotting history help separate the two tall, long-limbed patients.
whyNot: High pressure does not dislodge a lens. The order runs the other way: a dislocated lens can block aqueous flow and then raise the pressure.
Correct.
Ciliary muscle contraction relaxes the zonules so the lens can round up for near vision. It does not pull the lens out of its normal position.
Sorbitol buildup in the lens causes cataracts in diabetes, and galactitol does the same in galactosemia. These sugar alcohols cloud the lens without moving it.

topics: Ectopia lentis in homocystinuria versus Marfan syndrome

questions.stem: She is started on pyridoxine, a methionine-restricted diet, folic acid, and vitamin B12 to lower her plasma homocysteine. Vitamin B12 helps lower homocysteine by serving as a cofactor for which of the following enzymes?
options: Cystathionine beta-synthase
Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase
Dihydrofolate reductase
Methionine synthase
approach: Vitamin B12 is a cofactor for only two human enzymes: methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.
Only one of these acts on homocysteine. Methionine synthase moves a methyl group from N5-methyltetrahydrofolate onto homocysteine, making methionine.
Supporting this remethylation step pulls homocysteine down even though her blocked enzyme is in the other branch.
questions.why: Homocysteine has two exits: remethylation to methionine by methionine synthase (needs B12 and folate) and transsulfuration to cystathionine by cystathionine beta-synthase (needs B6). Her transsulfuration branch is blocked, so keeping the B12 and folate-dependent remethylation branch fully supplied helps clear homocysteine. The other B12 enzyme, methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, explains why methylmalonic acid rises in true B12 deficiency. Her normal B12 level and a normal methylmalonic acid would argue against B12 deficiency as the cause of her high homocysteine, while folate deficiency raises homocysteine alone and spares the nervous system.
whyNot: Cystathionine beta-synthase is the enzyme she lacks. It uses pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6), which is why pyridoxine is part of her treatment.
Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase does need vitamin B12, but it converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA and has no role in homocysteine metabolism.
Dihydrofolate reductase regenerates tetrahydrofolate using NADPH. It needs no vitamin B12 and is the target of methotrexate.
Correct.

questions.stem: Before her lens displacement was recognized, her blurred distance vision had been corrected with concave (minus) spectacle lenses. Which of the following best explains her refractive error?
options: Lax zonules letting the lens become more convex
Taut zonules holding the lens flatter than normal
An eyeball too short for its focusing power
Loss of lens elasticity with poor accommodation
approach: Blurred distance vision corrected by a concave lens means myopia: light focuses in front of the retina because the eye has too much focusing power.
Lens shape is set by zonular tension. Tight zonules flatten the lens, and slack zonules let it round up, as during accommodation for near vision.
Weak, lax zonules leave the lens rounder than normal all the time, adding focusing power and producing myopia.
questions.why: When the zonules lose tension, the elastic lens takes on a more spherical shape. A more convex lens bends light more strongly, so distant images focus in front of the retina. This lenticular myopia is often the first eye sign of homocystinuria, appearing before frank dislocation. The mechanism matches normal accommodation, where ciliary muscle contraction slackens the zonules so the lens can round up for near objects.
whyNot: Correct.
A flatter lens has less focusing power. That would push the focal point behind the retina and cause hyperopia, which blurs near vision first.
A short eyeball causes axial hyperopia. A convex (plus) lens corrects it, and here the correction was concave.
Loss of lens elasticity is presbyopia. It blurs near vision in middle age and is corrected with reading (plus) lenses.

questions.stem: At age 14 years, she is brought to the emergency department because of sudden severe pain in the right eye, headache, and vomiting. Intraocular pressure in the right eye is 54 mm Hg (normal 10 to 21). The right lens has moved forward into the pupil. Which of the following best explains the increase in intraocular pressure?
options: Increased aqueous secretion by the ciliary epithelium
Blocked tear outflow through the nasolacrimal duct
Aqueous trapped behind the iris, away from the angle
Excess tear secretion by the lacrimal gland
approach: Trace aqueous humor: secreted by the ciliary epithelium into the posterior chamber, through the pupil into the anterior chamber, then out through the trabecular meshwork and canal of Schlemm at the iridocorneal angle.
A lens wedged in the pupil plugs the only passage from the posterior chamber to the anterior chamber.
Secretion continues, fluid builds up behind the iris, the iris bows forward and closes the angle, and pressure rises sharply.
questions.why: This is pupillary block. Aqueous humor is made behind the iris and must pass through the pupil to reach its drainage site in the angle. When the dislocated lens blocks the pupil, aqueous collects in the posterior chamber, pushes the peripheral iris forward against the trabecular meshwork, and causes acute angle-closure glaucoma. Anterior lens dislocation with pupillary block is a known emergency in homocystinuria.
whyNot: Ciliary epithelial secretion is not increased by lens displacement. The problem is outflow, while secretion goes on at its usual rate.
The nasolacrimal duct drains tears from the surface of the eye into the nose. Tear flow never enters the eye and does not affect intraocular pressure.
Correct.
The lacrimal gland, driven by CN VII parasympathetic fibers, makes the watery layer of the tear film on the outside of the eye. Its output cannot raise pressure inside the globe.

case: A 47-year-old man comes to the physician because of double vision and drooping eyelids for 3 months. The symptoms are mild in the morning and worse by evening, and he has trouble chewing toward the end of meals. Physical examination shows bilateral ptosis that worsens during 60 seconds of sustained upward gaze and fatigable weakness of the neck flexors. Pupillary responses, sensation, and deep tendon reflexes are normal. Serum antibodies to the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor are positive. CT of the chest shows a 5-cm anterior mediastinal mass, and biopsy confirms a thymoma. He is diagnosed with myasthenia gravis associated with thymoma, and thymectomy is planned.

questions.stem: The immune mechanism causing this patient's weakness belongs to the same hypersensitivity category as the mechanism of which of the following disorders?
options: Multiple sclerosis
Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis
Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis
approach: First classify his disease. IgG antibodies bind a fixed antigen on a cell surface (the acetylcholine receptor), which is type II hypersensitivity.
Then classify each option. Look for another disease in which antibody binds a fixed membrane protein.
Lambert-Eaton syndrome uses IgG against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, also type II.
questions.why: Type II hypersensitivity is antibody directed against an antigen fixed on a cell or tissue. In myasthenia gravis the target is the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor; antibodies block it, cause its internalization, and fix complement to damage the end plate. Lambert-Eaton syndrome is the presynaptic counterpart, with antibodies to P/Q-type calcium channels on the motor nerve terminal. Both are type II despite affecting opposite sides of the synapse.
whyNot: Multiple sclerosis is driven mainly by autoreactive T cells against CNS myelin antigens, which is type IV hypersensitivity.
Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis is a postinfectious T cell-mediated attack on CNS myelin, also type IV.
Correct.
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis results from circulating immune complexes deposited in glomeruli, which is type III hypersensitivity.

questions.stem: Repetitive stimulation of the ulnar nerve at 3 Hz produces a progressive decline in compound muscle action potential amplitude over the first four to five responses. Which of the following best explains this decline in this patient?
options: Falling quantal release acting on too few receptors
Reduced calcium entry into the motor nerve terminal
Slowed conduction along demyelinated motor axons
Impaired calcium release from sarcoplasmic reticulum
approach: Normal transmission: an action potential opens calcium channels in the terminal, SNARE proteins fuse vesicles, and acetylcholine binds nicotinic receptors to make an end plate potential well above threshold (the safety factor).
During repeated stimulation, the number of vesicles released per impulse normally falls over the first few shocks. A healthy junction has enough spare receptors that every fiber still fires.
With antibody loss of receptors, the safety factor is small, so the normal fall in release drops more end plate potentials below threshold and fewer fibers contract.
questions.why: Acetylcholine receptor antibodies reduce the number of working postsynaptic receptors. Each end plate potential is therefore smaller, with little margin above threshold. Repetitive stimulation at a low rate depletes the readily releasable vesicle pool a little with each impulse, which is harmless in a normal muscle. In myasthenia gravis this ordinary decline pushes more fibers below threshold, so the summed muscle action potential shrinks, matching his fatigable weakness.
whyNot: Correct.

Reduced calcium entry is the Lambert-Eaton mechanism. It also shows a decrement at low rates, but this patient has receptor antibodies, normal reflexes, and a thymoma, which point to a postsynaptic defect.
Demyelination slows conduction and can cause conduction block, as in Guillain-Barre syndrome. It does not produce fatigable weakness with receptor antibodies.
Calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum is part of excitation-contraction coupling inside the muscle fiber. It does not change the muscle action potential recorded here.

questions.stem: He is started on pyridostigmine, and his ptosis improves. Which of the following reactions does this drug slow at the neuromuscular junction?
options: Transfer of an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to choline
Reuptake of intact acetylcholine into the nerve terminal
Transport of acetylcholine into synaptic vesicles
Hydrolysis of acetylcholine to choline and acetate
approach: Pyridostigmine is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, used to help the remaining receptors in myasthenia gravis.
Acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic cleft splits acetylcholine into choline and acetate, which ends its action.
Slowing this hydrolysis lets each released acetylcholine molecule bind receptors longer and more often, raising the end plate potential.
questions.why: Acetylcholine is made in the nerve terminal by choline acetyltransferase from acetyl-CoA and choline, packed into vesicles, and released into the cleft. Its action ends by rapid hydrolysis by acetylcholinesterase, and the freed choline is taken back up into the terminal for reuse. Pyridostigmine blocks acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine stays in the cleft longer and can activate more of the receptors that remain.
whyNot: This is the choline acetyltransferase reaction that synthesizes acetylcholine. Pyridostigmine does not block synthesis, and blocking it would worsen weakness.
Acetylcholine itself is not taken back up. The terminal recaptures choline after hydrolysis, using a high-affinity choline transporter.
Vesicular loading uses the vesicular acetylcholine transporter, which pyridostigmine does not affect.
Correct.

questions.stem: Thymoma-associated myasthenia gravis is classed as a paraneoplastic neurologic syndrome, in which a tumor triggers an immune response that also attacks the nervous system. Which of the following tumor and neurologic finding pairs arises by this type of mechanism?
options: Pituitary adenoma with bitemporal hemianopia
Ovarian teratoma with psychosis and dyskinesias
Small cell lung cancer with hyponatremic seizures
Apical lung cancer with ipsilateral Horner syndrome
approach: Define the mechanism: the tumor expresses a protein shared with neurons, and the antibody or T cell response against the tumor cross-reacts with the nervous system.
Sort the options by how the tumor causes the neurologic finding: direct compression or invasion, hormone secretion, or autoimmunity.
Ovarian teratomas contain neural tissue expressing NMDA receptors, and antibodies to these receptors cause anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.
questions.why: Neurologic paraneoplastic syndromes arise when tumors express neural antigens and the immune response against the tumor attacks neurons as well. In anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, an ovarian teratoma triggers antibodies to NMDA receptors, producing psychiatric symptoms, seizures, orofacial dyskinesias, and autonomic instability that often improve after the tumor is removed. Other examples are anti-Hu with small cell lung cancer and anti-Yo with cerebellar degeneration. In this patient, the thymoma likewise drives an autoimmune response, here against acetylcholine receptors.
whyNot: A pituitary adenoma growing upward compresses the optic chiasm. This is a direct mass effect with no immune component.
Correct.
Small cell lung cancer can secrete ADH (SIADH), and the resulting hyponatremia causes seizures. That is ectopic hormone production, a different paraneoplastic mechanism.
An apical (Pancoast) tumor invades the cervical sympathetic chain. This is local invasion with no immune component.

dx: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy during natalizumab therapy for multiple sclerosis
case: A 39-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis comes to the physician because of progressive difficulty speaking and clumsiness of the right hand over 5 weeks. She has received monthly natalizumab infusions for 3 years, and serum antibodies to JC virus were positive before treatment began. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse 70/min, respirations 14/min, and blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg. Physical examination shows weakness of the right hand and a language disturbance. MRI of the brain shows new asymmetric, nonenhancing T2-hyperintense lesions in the subcortical white matter of the left frontal and parietal lobes without mass effect. PCR of the cerebrospinal fluid detects JC virus DNA. She is diagnosed with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, and natalizumab is stopped.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the virus that caused this patient's disease and its usual site of latency?
options: Nonenveloped dsDNA virus latent in the kidney
Enveloped dsDNA virus latent in sensory ganglia
Enveloped ssRNA virus latent in CD4+ T cells
Enveloped dsDNA virus latent in B lymphocytes
approach: PML is caused by JC virus, a polyomavirus.
Polyomaviruses are small, nonenveloped, double-stranded DNA viruses.
Most people are infected in childhood without symptoms, and the virus stays latent in the kidney (it is shed in urine) until severe immunosuppression lets it reactivate.
questions.why: JC virus is a nonenveloped dsDNA polyomavirus. Primary infection is silent and common, which is why most adults, including this patient, have antibodies. The virus persists in the kidney and lymphoid tissue. When cellular immunity falls, as with AIDS, natalizumab, or rituximab, it reactivates, reaches the brain, and infects oligodendrocytes.
whyNot: Correct.
This describes herpes simplex and varicella zoster viruses, which hide in sensory ganglion neurons and travel along axons when they reactivate.
This describes HIV, a retrovirus whose integrated provirus persists in resting memory CD4+ T cells. HIV raises PML risk but does not cause the lesions.
This describes Epstein-Barr virus, a herpesvirus latent in memory B cells. It is linked to primary CNS lymphoma, which forms enhancing masses.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why this patient's lesions are confined to the white matter?
options: Autoantibodies to myelin basic protein
Infarction of deep penetrating arterioles
Lytic infection of oligodendrocytes
T cell attack on myelin after a viral illness
approach: White matter is made of axons wrapped in myelin, and in the CNS the myelin is made by oligodendrocytes.
JC virus selectively infects and kills oligodendrocytes (and also infects astrocytes).
Each dead oligodendrocyte strips myelin from many axons, so lesions spread through white matter and leave the cortex relatively spared.
questions.why: In PML, reactivated JC virus enters oligodendrocytes and destroys them, producing patchy demyelination that enlarges and merges. Infected oligodendrocyte nuclei look enlarged and glassy, and nearby astrocytes can look bizarre. Because the immune system is suppressed, there is little inflammation, so the lesions usually do not enhance or cause mass effect, and deficits worsen over weeks.
whyNot: Myelin antibodies are not the cause of PML. The damage comes from direct viral killing of the cells that make myelin.
Deep arteriolar infarcts cause lacunar strokes with sudden deficits. They do not progress steadily over weeks or contain viral DNA.
Correct.
A T cell attack on myelin after an infection describes acute disseminated encephalomyelitis. That needs an active immune response, which natalizumab blunts.

questions.stem: Her speech is fluent with frequent phonemic errors, and she correctly follows spoken three-step commands. She cannot repeat a short phrase spoken by the examiner. Damage to which of the following structures most likely explains her language disturbance?
options: Posterior inferior frontal gyrus
Arcuate fasciculus
Posterior superior temporal gyrus
Precentral gyrus face area
approach: Sort the aphasia with three checks: fluency, comprehension, and repetition. Fluent speech with intact comprehension and impaired repetition is conduction aphasia.
Repetition requires sound heard in Wernicke area to reach Broca area. The arcuate fasciculus is the white matter tract that links them.
A white matter disease such as PML in the left parietal lobe can cut this tract while sparing both cortical language areas.
questions.why: Conduction aphasia leaves fluency and comprehension intact because both Broca and Wernicke areas still work, but the two cannot communicate. The patient understands the phrase and can speak, yet cannot repeat it, and makes sound-substitution (phonemic) errors. The responsible lesion lies in the arcuate fasciculus, which runs deep to the supramarginal gyrus in the dominant parietal lobe, matching her left parietal white matter lesion.
whyNot: Damage to the posterior inferior frontal gyrus (Broca area) causes nonfluent, effortful speech with good comprehension, and her speech is fluent.
Correct.
Damage to the posterior superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke area) causes fluent speech with poor comprehension, and she follows commands correctly.
Damage to the face area of the precentral gyrus causes dysarthria and lower facial weakness. Language content and repetition stay normal.

questions.stem: Natalizumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds alpha-4 integrin. Which of the following best explains how this drug allowed the virus to reactivate in her brain?
options: Depletion of resident microglia by antibody-mediated lysis
Loss of tight junctions between brain capillary endothelial cells
Inhibited IL-1 and TNF release by microglia
Blocked lymphocyte adhesion to brain capillary endothelium
approach: Alpha-4 integrin sits on lymphocytes and lets them bind VCAM-1 on activated endothelium, the first step in crossing into tissue.

The blood-brain barrier, with tight junctions between endothelial cells, keeps most immune cells out. Resident microglia handle innate defense, but control of latent viruses depends on T cells that patrol the brain.
Blocking alpha-4 integrin stops T cells from entering the CNS, so JC virus can replicate unchecked.
questions.why: The CNS has limited immune surveillance. Its blood-brain barrier restricts entry, and its resident innate cells are microglia. Adaptive control of viruses depends on lymphocytes that cross the endothelium by binding adhesion molecules. Natalizumab blocks alpha-4 integrin, which reduces MS relapses by keeping autoreactive T cells out, but it also keeps out the cytotoxic T cells that hold JC virus in check. Risk rises with positive JC antibodies, longer treatment, and prior immunosuppressant use.
whyNot: Natalizumab blocks cell adhesion without killing cells. Resident microglia remain present during treatment.
Loss of endothelial tight junctions increases barrier permeability, as with cytokines in bacterial meningitis. That would let more cells into the brain.
Natalizumab does not block cytokine release by microglia. IL-1 and TNF are the cytokines that open the barrier in bacterial meningitis.
Correct.

topics: Blood-brain barrier and CNS immune surveillance

dx: Neurocysticercosis with new-onset seizures and obstructive hydrocephalus
case: A 26-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. For 3 weeks he has had morning headaches and vomiting. He moved to the United States from a rural area of southern Mexico 2 years ago. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse 74/min, respirations 14/min, and blood pressure 134/82 mm Hg. Funduscopic examination shows bilateral papilledema. CT of the brain shows several small calcified parenchymal lesions. MRI shows a parenchymal cyst with an eccentric scolex and a separate intraventricular cyst with hydrocephalus. A serum immunoblot for Taenia solium antibodies is positive. He is diagnosed with neurocysticercosis with seizures and hydrocephalus.

questions.stem: He reports that he has never eaten pork. Which of the following is the most likely way he acquired this infection?
options: Eating cysts in undercooked pork
Skin penetration by larvae in soil
Nasal entry of amebae from fresh water
Swallowing eggs from human feces
approach: Separate the two diseases Taenia solium causes. Eating larval cysts in undercooked pork gives an adult tapeworm in the gut (taeniasis).
Swallowing eggs shed in the feces of a human tapeworm carrier gives cysticercosis. Larvae hatch, cross the gut wall, and lodge as cysts in brain, muscle, and eye.
Neurocysticercosis therefore needs no pork, only fecal contamination of food or water by a human carrier.
questions.why: Humans are the definitive host of Taenia solium, carrying the adult worm after eating cysticerci in pork. When a person instead ingests the eggs, the human acts like an intermediate host and cysticerci form in tissues. In the brain, living cysts can sit quietly for years, and degenerating or calcified cysts provoke inflammation and seizures. It is a leading cause of acquired epilepsy in endemic regions.
whyNot: Eating cysts in undercooked pork causes intestinal taeniasis with an adult worm in the gut. It does not by itself place cysts in the brain, and he has never eaten pork.
Larvae that penetrate skin from soil describe hookworm and Strongyloides, which do not form brain cysts.
Entry of amebae through the nose and cribriform plate after freshwater swimming describes Naegleria fowleri, which causes a rapidly fatal meningoencephalitis.
Correct.

questions.stem: MRI shows marked dilation of both lateral ventricles and the third ventricle, while the fourth ventricle is normal in size. The intraventricular cyst is most likely lodged in which of the following?
options: Left interventricular foramen
Cerebral aqueduct
Foramina of Luschka and Magendie
Arachnoid granulations
approach: Trace CSF: choroid plexus in the lateral ventricles, through the interventricular foramina to the third ventricle, through the cerebral aqueduct to the fourth ventricle, then out the foramina of Luschka and Magendie into the subarachnoid space.
Ventricles upstream of a block dilate, and those downstream stay normal.
Both lateral ventricles and the third ventricle are large and the fourth is normal, so the block sits between the third and fourth ventricles: the cerebral aqueduct.
questions.why: The cerebral aqueduct is the narrowest part of the ventricular system, so a small cyst can plug it. CSF from both lateral ventricles and the third ventricle cannot reach the fourth ventricle, so all three enlarge while the fourth stays normal. Raised pressure explains his morning headaches, vomiting, and papilledema.
whyNot: A block at one interventricular foramen (of Monro) would enlarge only the lateral ventricle on that side, leaving the third ventricle normal.
Correct.
A block at the fourth ventricle outlets would enlarge the fourth ventricle along with the lateral and third ventricles.
Failure of absorption at the arachnoid granulations causes communicating hydrocephalus, with all four ventricles enlarged.

topics: Predicting ventricular dilation from the site of obstruction

questions.stem: This patient's hydrocephalus belongs to the same category as hydrocephalus caused by which of the following?
options: Scarring of arachnoid granulations after meningitis
Cortical atrophy in advanced Alzheimer disease
Dandy-Walker malformation
Idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus
approach: Classify his case first. A cyst inside the ventricular system blocks flow before CSF reaches the subarachnoid space, so this is noncommunicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus.
Then classify each option. Communicating hydrocephalus means CSF reaches the subarachnoid space but is not absorbed. Ex vacuo means ventricles enlarge passively because brain tissue is lost.
Dandy-Walker malformation blocks the outflow of the fourth ventricle, another noncommunicating cause.
questions.why: Noncommunicating hydrocephalus comes from a block within the ventricles or at their exits. Causes include aqueductal stenosis, Chiari II and Dandy-Walker malformations, tumors, and intraventricular cysts like this one. Communicating hydrocephalus follows scarring of the arachnoid granulations after meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage. Hydrocephalus ex vacuo is enlargement of the ventricles to fill space left by atrophy, with normal pressure and no flow problem.
whyNot: Arachnoid granulation scarring after meningitis impairs absorption while flow through the ventricles stays open. That is communicating hydrocephalus.
Ventricles enlarge in Alzheimer disease because the brain shrinks. That is hydrocephalus ex vacuo, with no obstruction and no raised pressure.
Correct.
Normal pressure hydrocephalus is a communicating form in older adults, with all ventricles enlarged and open pathways, causing gait problems, incontinence, and dementia.

questions.stem: Several hours after admission, he becomes drowsy, and intracranial pressure is 32 mm Hg (normal 5 to 15). While a ventricular drain is prepared, he is intubated and ventilated to an arterial PCO2 of 30 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45). Which of the following best explains how this ventilation lowers his intracranial pressure?
options: Cerebral arteriolar constriction lowering blood volume
Increased CSF absorption at the arachnoid granulations
Reduced CSF secretion by the choroid plexus
Dilation of cerebral arterioles improving perfusion
approach: The skull is a fixed box holding brain, CSF, and blood. Lowering any one of these lowers pressure.
Cerebral arterioles respond strongly to PaCO2: high CO2 dilates them, and low CO2 constricts them.
Hyperventilation lowers PaCO2, the arterioles constrict, cerebral blood volume falls, and intracranial pressure drops within minutes.
questions.why: Cerebral blood flow is held fairly steady across a wide range of blood pressure (autoregulation), but it changes sharply with PaCO2. A lower PaCO2 raises the pH around the arterioles, which constrict, reducing the volume of blood inside the skull. This buys time while the drain is placed. The effect is short-lived, and too much constriction can cause ischemia, so it is a bridge only. Cerebral perfusion pressure equals mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure, so lowering ICP also helps restore perfusion.
whyNot: Correct.

CSF absorption depends on the pressure difference between the subarachnoid space and the venous sinuses. A lower PaCO2 does not open the arachnoid granulations, and his CSF cannot reach them past the block anyway.
Choroid plexus secretion is reduced by drugs such as acetazolamide. A short drop in PaCO2 does not meaningfully change CSF production.
Arteriolar dilation is the response to high PaCO2. It would add blood volume and raise intracranial pressure.

dx: Early disseminated Lyme disease with bilateral facial nerve palsy
case: A 31-year-old man comes to the physician because of inability to close either eye completely and drooling from both corners of his mouth for 6 days. He also has headache and mild neck stiffness. He lives in northern Wisconsin and hunts in wooded areas. Five weeks ago, he had an expanding red rash on his back that faded without treatment. Temperature is 37.6 °C (99.7 °F), pulse 76/min, respirations 14/min, and blood pressure 122/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows weakness of all muscles of facial expression on both sides, including the forehead. Limb strength, sensation, and reflexes are normal. Two-tier serologic testing for Borrelia burgdorferi is positive. He is diagnosed with early disseminated Lyme disease with bilateral facial nerve palsy.

questions.stem: The organism that caused this patient's disease has the same basic morphology as which of the following organisms?
options: Mycobacterium leprae
Treponema pallidum
Rickettsia rickettsii
Anaplasma phagocytophilum
approach: Borrelia burgdorferi is a spirochete: a thin, helical bacterium that moves with internal (periplasmic) flagella.
Look for another spirochete among the options.
Treponema pallidum, the cause of syphilis, is also a spirochete, though it is too thin for routine stains and is seen with darkfield microscopy.
questions.why: Spirochetes that cause human disease include Borrelia, Treponema, and Leptospira. Borrelia burgdorferi is carried by Ixodes ticks, with white-footed mice as the main reservoir. Treponema pallidum is diagnosed with darkfield microscopy and serology (VDRL then FTA-ABS), and both organisms can involve the nervous system. Sharing a vector with Borrelia does not make an organism a spirochete.
whyNot: Mycobacterium leprae is an acid-fast rod that grows best in cooler body sites and infects Schwann cells. Its US reservoir is the armadillo.
Correct.
Rickettsia rickettsii is an obligate intracellular gram-negative coccobacillus spread by Dermacentor ticks. It causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
Anaplasma phagocytophilum is also spread by Ixodes ticks, but it is a small obligate intracellular bacterium that grows inside neutrophils.

questions.stem: A lumbar puncture is performed. Which of the following cerebrospinal fluid findings are most likely?
options: Lymphocytes, normal glucose, mild protein rise
Neutrophils, low glucose, high protein
Normal cell count, normal glucose, high protein
Lymphocytes, low glucose, very high protein
approach: Headache, neck stiffness, and cranial nerve palsies weeks after erythema migrans point to Lyme neuroborreliosis: lymphocytic meningitis, cranial neuritis, and radiculopathy.
Lyme meningitis behaves like an aseptic (viral-type) meningitis: lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, and modestly raised protein.
Low glucose suggests bacterial, tuberculous, or fungal meningitis, and very high protein with normal cells suggests Guillain-Barre syndrome.
questions.why: Borrelia spreads through the blood weeks after the tick bite and can seed the meninges and cranial nerves. The facial nerve is the cranial nerve most often involved, and Lyme disease is one of the few common causes of bilateral facial palsy. The CSF shows a lymphocytic meningitis with normal glucose and a mild to moderate protein rise. Intrathecal antibody production against Borrelia can confirm CNS involvement.
whyNot: Correct.
A neutrophil-predominant CSF with low glucose is acute bacterial meningitis from pyogenic organisms. His course over weeks and positive Borrelia serology do not fit.
High protein with a normal cell count is the albuminocytologic dissociation of Guillain-Barre syndrome, which can also cause bilateral facial palsy, but his limb strength and reflexes are normal.
Lymphocytes with low glucose and very high protein suggest tuberculous or fungal meningitis, which usually affects basal cranial nerves with a more severe illness.

questions.stem: A small infarct of the face area of one motor cortex would weaken only the contralateral lower face and spare the forehead. Which of the following best explains why a cortical lesion spares the forehead while this patient's facial nerve lesions do not?
options: The forehead muscles are supplied by the trigeminal nerve
Lower face motor neurons receive input from both hemispheres
Corticobulbar fibers to the upper face do not cross
Upper face motor neurons receive input from both hemispheres
approach: In the facial motor nucleus, the neurons for the upper face get corticobulbar input from both hemispheres, while those for the lower face get input mainly from the opposite hemisphere.
A cortical lesion removes only one of the two inputs to the upper face, so the forehead keeps working.
A lesion of the facial nerve itself cuts the final common pathway to every muscle of facial expression, so the forehead is weak too.
questions.why: Because the forehead motor neurons have bilateral cortical input, an upper motor neuron lesion spares the forehead and weakens only the contralateral lower face. A lower motor neuron lesion of CN VII, such as Lyme facial neuritis, involves every muscle on that side, including the frontalis and orbicularis oculi. In this patient both nerves are affected, so the whole face is weak on both sides.
whyNot: The frontalis is a muscle of facial expression and is supplied by the temporal branch of the facial nerve. The trigeminal nerve carries forehead sensation and supplies the muscles of mastication.
This reverses the pattern. Lower face motor neurons get input mainly from the opposite cortex, which is why a cortical lesion weakens the contralateral lower face.
Upper face corticobulbar fibers come from both sides, with both crossed and uncrossed fibers. If they were only uncrossed, a cortical infarct would weaken the forehead on the same side.
Correct.

questions.stem: Before the serologic results were available, he was started on empiric ceftriaxone and vancomycin to cover the most common cause of bacterial meningitis in previously healthy adults of his age. Which of the following organisms is this regimen chiefly directed against?
options: Escherichia coli K1
Streptococcus agalactiae
Streptococcus pneumoniae
Listeria monocytogenes
approach: Place the patient in an age group. He is a healthy adult younger than 50 years.
In children and adults, the leading bacterial causes of meningitis are Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis.
Vancomycin is added to ceftriaxone mainly to cover penicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae, the most common cause in adults.
questions.why: The likely bacteria in meningitis shift with age. Neonates get group B streptococcus, E. coli, and Listeria from the birth canal. Children and adults get S. pneumoniae and N. meningitidis, with S. pneumoniae the most common cause in adults. Older adults add Listeria back, which is why ampicillin is added after about age 50 years. Ceftriaxone with vancomycin covers both pneumococcus, including resistant strains, and meningococcus.
whyNot: E. coli K1 is a leading cause of meningitis in neonates, acquired from the maternal birth canal. It is uncommon in healthy adults.
Streptococcus agalactiae (group B streptococcus) is the most common cause of neonatal meningitis. It rarely causes meningitis in healthy young adults.
Correct.
Listeria causes meningitis in neonates, adults older than about 50 years, and immunocompromised patients. It is resistant to cephalosporins and would need ampicillin, which was not given.
